%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\subsubsection{Benchmark Redundancy Analysis}
\label{app:benchpress}
%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%

We adapt the BenchPress methodology~\cite{papailiopoulos2026benchpress} to quantify redundancy among benchmarks and to test whether agent scaffolding introduces structure beyond model capability alone.  BenchPress was originally applied to an 83-model $\times$ 49-benchmark matrix (34\% filled), with core analyses on a fully-observed 31$\times$10 subblock.  Our setting differs in three respects: the matrix is \AppNumSystems{}~systems $\times$ \AppNumBenchmarks{}~benchmarks (fully observed after coverage filtering); rows include both baseline and scaffolded systems; and scores are task-aggregate benchmark scores on each benchmark's native metric scale.  All included benchmarks have scores in $[0,1]$; benchmarks with unbounded scales (e.g., MLGym) are excluded from the logit-space analyses described below.

\paragraph{Methodology.}
Percentage-bounded scores $s \in [0,1]$ are transformed to logit space:
\begin{equation}
  z = \operatorname{logit}(s) = \log\!\frac{\,\mathrm{clip}(s,\,\epsilon,\,1{-}\epsilon)\,}
       {1 - \mathrm{clip}(s,\,\epsilon,\,1{-}\epsilon)},
  \quad \epsilon = 0.005,
  \label{eq:logit}
\end{equation}
where $s$ is the raw benchmark score (pass rate or normalized metric), $z$ is the logit-transformed score used in all subsequent regression and SVD analyses, and $\epsilon$ clips extreme values away from 0 and 1 to avoid infinite logits.

The predictor blends two components:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{LogitBenchReg.} For each target benchmark~$b_j$, select the $k{=}5$ other benchmarks with the highest training-set $R^2$ via univariate OLS in logit space (minimum $R^2 \ge 0.1$).  Predict the held-out system as the $R^2$-weighted average of univariate predictions, inverse-logit-transformed.

\item \textbf{SVD-Logit (Soft-Impute).}  Column-wise $z$-score the logit matrix, initialize missing entries to~0, then iterate rank-$r$ truncated SVD---replacing only missing entries with the low-rank approximation---until convergence ($\Delta_{\mathrm{rel}} < 10^{-4}$).  De-standardize and inverse-logit to obtain predictions.
\end{enumerate}

The final predictor is
$\hat{s} = 0.6 \times \hat{s}^{\mathrm{BenchReg}} + 0.4 \times \hat{s}^{\mathrm{SVD}}$,
following~\cite{papailiopoulos2026benchpress}.  When LogitBenchReg produces no prediction, the method falls back to SVD-Logit alone; when both fail, it falls back to the column mean.

\paragraph{Evaluation protocol.}
Per-system holdout: for each of 5 random seeds, randomly mask 50\% of each system's scores, train on the remainder, and predict the masked cells.  The primary metric is Median Absolute Percentage Error (MedAPE):
\begin{equation}
  \mathrm{MedAPE} = \operatorname{median}_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{H}}
    \frac{|\hat{s}_{i,j} - s_{i,j}|}{|s_{i,j}|} \times 100\%,
  \label{eq:medape}
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal{H}$ is the set of held-out (masked) cells, $i$ indexes systems (model--agent pairs), $j$ indexes benchmarks, $s_{i,j}$ is the observed score for system $i$ on benchmark $j$, and $\hat{s}_{i,j}$ is the predicted score.

\paragraph{Low-rank structure.}
\textit{A single capability axis dominates model-only evaluation; adding scaffolds introduces an orthogonal dimension.}
SVD in logit space on the \AppNumModelsOnly{}-system Terminus-2 submatrix (varying only the base model under a fixed minimal scaffold) yields PC1 = \AppSVDModelOnlyPCOne{}\% of variance---comparable to BenchPress's 71\% on their 31$\times$10 block with scaffold-free evaluations.  The first two components capture \AppSVDModelOnlyPCOneTwo{}\%, confirming that the benchmark space is dominated by a single ``general capability'' axis across \AppNumModelsOnly{}~frontier models.

On the full \AppNumSystems{}-system matrix, the spectrum shifts: PC1 drops to \AppSVDFullPCOne{}\% and PC2 captures \AppSVDFullPCTwo{}\% (cumulative \AppSVDFullCumTwo{}\%).  Figure~\ref{fig:svd-spectrum} visualizes the comparison.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figs/appendix/quantitative/benchmark_svd_spectrum}
  \caption{Singular value spectrum of the benchmark score matrix in logit space.  Blue: \AppNumModelsOnly{}-system Terminus-2 submatrix (baseline scaffold only).  Purple: full \AppNumSystems{}-system matrix (all scaffolds).  The drop in PC1 share and rise in PC2 when scaffolds are included reflects the orthogonal ``agent effect'' dimension.}
  \label{fig:svd-spectrum}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Agent separation in PC2.}
\textit{The second principal component achieves perfect separation between scaffolded and baseline systems.}
On the full matrix, PC2 separates the \AppNumAgentSystems{} advanced-scaffold systems (mean $= {}\AppPCTwoAgentMean{}$) from the \AppNumBaseSystems{} Terminus-2 baselines (mean $= {}\AppPCTwoBaseMean{}$) with zero overlap.  This orthogonal ``agent effect'' dimension is invisible in model-only matrices, which is why BenchPress's original analysis reported a single dominant component.

\paragraph{Prediction accuracy.}
\textit{The BenchPress blend reduces prediction error by \AppBlendImprovement{}\% over the column-mean baseline.}

\begin{table}[h]\small
\centering
\caption{Prediction methods on our \AppNumSystems{}$\times$\AppNumBenchmarks{} matrix (50\% holdout, 5~seeds).}
\label{tab:benchpress-methods}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Method & MedAPE (\%) & MedAE \\
\midrule
Column mean (baseline) & \AppBaselineMedAPE{} & \AppBaselineMedAE{} \\
LogitBenchReg only     & \AppLogitBenchRegMedAPE{} & \AppLogitBenchRegMedAE{} \\
SVD-Logit ($r{=}2$)    & \AppSVDLogitMedAPE{} & \AppSVDLogitMedAE{} \\
BenchPress blend ($r{=}2$) & \textbf{\AppBlendMedAPE{}} & \textbf{\AppBlendMedAE{}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The blend achieves \AppBlendMedAPE{}\% MedAPE---higher than BenchPress's 7\% on their larger matrix, which we attribute to our smaller system count (\AppNumSystems{} vs.\ 31 rows) and substantially greater benchmark diversity (\AppNumBenchmarks{} vs.\ 10 columns).

\paragraph{Per-benchmark predictability.}
\textit{Predictability identifies redundancy: benchmarks that are easily predicted from others provide no independent signal.}

\AppPerBenchmarkPredictTable{}

Benchmarks that resist prediction---\BenchPressUniqueOne{} (\BenchPressUniqueOneScore{}\%), \BenchPressUniqueTwo{} (\BenchPressUniqueTwoScore{}\%), \BenchPressUniqueThree{} (\BenchPressUniqueThreeScore{}\%)---test capabilities orthogonal to the dominant axis: novel agentic research tasks, scientific experimentation, and abstract reasoning.  Conversely, highly predictable benchmarks like \BenchPressRedundantOne{} (\BenchPressRedundantOneScore{}\%) and \BenchPressRedundantTwo{} (\BenchPressRedundantTwoScore{}\%) are fully explained by the general-capability component.

\paragraph{Greedy forward selection.}
\label{par:greedy-selection}
\textit{Only \GreedyBenchmarksBelowSeven{} of \AppNumBenchmarks{} benchmarks contribute independent signal at the $|\rho|<0.7$ threshold.}
Greedy forward selection starts from the benchmark with the lowest mean absolute correlation to all others and iteratively adds the benchmark whose maximum absolute correlation with the already-selected set is smallest.  The first \GreedyBenchmarksBelowSeven{} selections all satisfy $\max|\rho| < 0.7$; from step~\GreedyFirstAboveSevenStep{} onward, every remaining benchmark has $|\rho| \ge 0.7$ with at least one already-selected benchmark.

The selection sequence:
\begin{enumerate}
\AppBenchGreedySequence{}
\end{enumerate}
The first redundant benchmark (\GreedyFirstAboveSeven{}, step~\GreedyFirstAboveSevenStep{}, $\rho{=}\GreedyFirstAboveSevenCorr{}$) is largely explained by the already-selected set.  For practitioners with constrained budgets, $\sim$\GreedyBenchmarksBelowSeven{} well-chosen benchmarks across domains capture most independent signal in the full \AppNumBenchmarks{}-benchmark suite.

\paragraph{Task-level SVD structure.}
\textit{Low-rank structure persists at the individual-task level, but benchmark aggregation compresses away independent dimensions.}
We extend the SVD analysis to the \AppNumSystems{}-system $\times$ \TaskGoodTasks{}-task matrix (after filtering \TaskZeroVarTasks{} zero-variance tasks where all systems scored identically).  Despite the high dimensionality and binary nature of many individual scores, the low-rank structure holds:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
    \item \textbf{PC1} (general capability): \TaskFullPCOne{}\% of variance across all systems (\TaskModelPCOne{}\% when restricted to \AppNumModelsOnly{} baselines).
    \item \textbf{PC2} (agent axis): \TaskFullPCTwo{}\% of variance, separating scaffolded (mean $= +\TaskAgentPCTwoMean{}$) from baseline systems (mean $= \TaskBasePCTwoMean{}$).
\end{itemize}
The spectrum contrast is informative: at the benchmark level PC1 captures \AppSVDFullPCOne{}\% of variance, whereas at the task level only \TaskFullPCOne{}\%---task-level evaluation preserves multiple independent dimensions that benchmark aggregation compresses away.

\paragraph{Intra-benchmark dimensionality.}
\textit{Individual benchmarks are internally low-rank: a handful of representative tasks suffice for reliable system ranking.}
For each of the \TaskRedundNumBenchmarks{} benchmarks with $\ge 10$ tasks, PCA on the \AppNumSystems{} $\times$ $T$ task matrix (after removing zero-variance tasks, averaging \TaskRedundMeanZeroVarPct{}\% per benchmark) shows that PC1 alone explains \TaskRedundMeanPCOne{}\% of within-benchmark variance on average, and a median of only \TaskRedundMedianPCsNinety{} components suffices for 90\%---a \TaskRedundMeanCompression{}$\times$ compression ratio.

Some benchmarks are particularly low-rank:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{\TaskLowRankExTwoName{}} (\TaskLowRankExTwoTasks{} tasks): PC1 = \TaskLowRankExTwoPCOne{}\%, only \TaskLowRankExTwoPCs{}~components for 90\%.
  \item \textbf{\TaskLowRankExThreeName{}} (\TaskLowRankExThreeTasks{} tasks): PC1 = \TaskLowRankExThreePCOne{}\%, \TaskLowRankExThreePCs{}~components for 90\%.
  \item \textbf{\TaskLowRankExOneName{}} (\TaskLowRankExOneTasks{} tasks): PC1 = \TaskLowRankExOnePCOne{}\%, \TaskLowRankExOnePCs{}~components for 90\%.
\end{itemize}
These benchmarks contain hundreds of items that essentially measure the same underlying capability axis.  We can also verify this via ranking fidelity: selecting the $k$ tasks with the highest Spearman correlation to the full benchmark mean score, the resulting $k$-task subset preserves the system ranking with high fidelity (Table~\ref{tab:task-redundancy}).

  \label{tab:task-redundancy}

    $k$ tasks & Mean $\rho$ & Benchmarks $\rho > 0.95$ & Typical reduction \\

With just 10 well-chosen tasks, \TaskRedundAboveNFKTen{} benchmarks achieve $\rho > 0.95$, and the overall mean $\rho$ across all benchmarks reaches \TaskRedundRhoKTen{} at $k{=}10$---indicating that a small task subset can approximate the full-suite ranking with high fidelity for most benchmarks.

\paragraph{Within-benchmark task holdout prediction.}
\label{par:task-holdout}
\textit{Peer-based prediction quantifies task redundancy directly: benchmarks with highly predictable items contain interchangeable measurement points.}
Applying full BenchPress across $\TaskGoodTasks{}$ tasks with only $\AppNumSystems{}{-}1$ training systems guarantees spurious fit.  We circumvent this by restricting prediction to tasks \emph{within the same benchmark}: for each benchmark with $\ge 5$ reliable tasks, we apply a holdout protocol within the $(\AppNumSystems{} \times T)$ sub-matrix---randomly masking 50\% of each system's scores (3 folds), predicting via (a)~task-mean baseline, (b)~top-$k$ peer-weighted correlation, and (c)~within-benchmark rank-2 SVD, then blending (b) and (c) at $0.6/0.4$.

Across \TaskHoldoutNumBenchmarks{} benchmarks, the blend improves over baseline in \TaskHoldoutNumImproved{} cases (median improvement \TaskHoldoutMedianImprovement{}\%).  The most internally predictable benchmarks---\TaskHoldoutBestOneName{} (\TaskHoldoutBestOneImp{}\%), \TaskHoldoutBestTwoName{} (\TaskHoldoutBestTwoImp{}\%), \TaskHoldoutBestThreeName{} (\TaskHoldoutBestThreeImp{}\%)---contain items that test essentially the same capability axis.  Benchmarks where the blend underperforms (e.g., \TaskHoldoutWorstOneName{}, \TaskHoldoutWorstTwoName{}) have heterogeneous task structures resistant to peer-based prediction.

\paragraph{Representative tasks and within-benchmark greedy selection.}
\label{par:per-bench-goto}
\textit{A single well-chosen task per benchmark can approximate the full-suite ranking; three tasks achieve $\rho \approx \TaskRedundRhoKThree{}$.}
Table~\ref{tab:go-to-tasks} lists the single most representative task per benchmark---the task whose leave-one-out correlation with the remaining-task aggregate is highest, weighted by task variance (``useful representativeness score'').

\AppGoToTaskTable{}

Mirroring the benchmark-level greedy selection, we apply greedy forward selection within each benchmark.  The fraction of tasks with $\max|\rho| < 0.7$ varies widely: \TaskGreedyHighIndepOneName{} (\TaskGreedyHighIndepOnePct{}\%) and \TaskGreedyHighIndepTwoName{} (\TaskGreedyHighIndepTwoPct{}\%) contain many independently-informative items, while \TaskGreedyLowIndepOneName{} and \TaskGreedyLowIndepTwoName{} reach $\rho > 0.7$ within the first few selections.

\paragraph{Within- vs.\ cross-benchmark prediction.}
\label{par:unified-holdout}
\textit{Same-benchmark peers predict better in most cases, but a substantial minority of benchmarks share latent structure across evaluation boundaries.}
We run a unified holdout comparison: for each benchmark, the same mask and $k{=}5$ peer count across three scopes (within-benchmark, cross-benchmark only, global pool), each blended with rank-2 SVD at $0.6/0.4$.

Within-benchmark blends outperform global blends in \UnifiedWithinBetter{}/\UnifiedHoldoutNumBenchmarks{} (\UnifiedWithinBetterPct{}\%) cases.  Median improvement over baseline: \UnifiedMedianWithinImp{}\% (within), \UnifiedMedianCrossImp{}\% (cross), \UnifiedMedianGlobalImp{}\% (global).  For the remaining \UnifiedCrossBetter{}/\UnifiedHoldoutNumBenchmarks{} benchmarks, cross-benchmark peers predict \emph{better}---indicating shared capability axes that cut across nominal evaluation boundaries.

\paragraph{Cross-benchmark global representative tasks.}
\label{par:global-goto}
\textit{Per-benchmark and cross-benchmark representativeness select different tasks---the overlap is only \GoToOverlapPct{}\%.}
We flatten all \GlobalGoToNumTasks{} reliable bounded tasks into a single pool and compute two measures: (1)~\emph{global representativeness} (leave-one-out correlation with the full-pool aggregate $\times$ task standard deviation), and (2)~\emph{greedy independence} (iteratively selecting the task least correlated with the already-selected set).

Table~\ref{tab:global-go-to-tasks} lists the top~25 tasks by global representativeness.  The greedy sequence begins with:
\begin{enumerate}
\AppGlobalGreedySequence{}
\end{enumerate}

\AppGlobalGoToTaskTable{}

Comparing per-benchmark top-1 tasks with the top-$N$ globally representative tasks yields only \GoToOverlapCount{}/\GoToOverlapTotal{} (\GoToOverlapPct{}\%) overlap.  Per-benchmark selection tracks \emph{within-benchmark} variation; global selection tracks the \emph{cross-benchmark consensus}.  Benchmarks with idiosyncratic profiles (those identified as ``unique'' in the predictability analysis) nominate internally representative tasks that appear unrepresentative in the global pool.

\paragraph{Combined go-to task set.}
\textit{A principled compact evaluation: \GoToSetNumTasks{} tasks across \GoToSetNumBenchmarks{} benchmarks balance independence with representativeness.}
Within each benchmark, greedy forward selection identifies independently informative tasks ($\max|\rho| < 0.7$); the top~3 by useful representativeness are retained.  This yields a \GoToSetNumTasks{}-task set---substantially reduced from the full \GlobalGoToNumTasks{}-task pool while preserving both within-benchmark coverage and cross-benchmark diversity.

\AppGoToTaskSetTable{}

\paragraph{Implications.}
Two-level redundancy---across benchmarks and within them---implies that a carefully selected subset of benchmarks, each evaluated on a small number of representative tasks, approximates the full evaluation matrix at a fraction of the computational cost.  The combined go-to task set (\GoToSetNumTasks{} tasks) provides a principled starting point for budget-constrained evaluation.

\subsubsection{Model vs.\ Agent Effect: Methodology}
\label{app:model-vs-agent}

We formalize the within-family and adjusted-effect analyses from Section~\ref{sec:agent-harness}.  Let $s(m, a, b)$ denote the benchmark-relative score for model~$m$, agent scaffold~$a$, and benchmark~$b$.

\paragraph{Within-family comparison.}
\label{app:within-family}

For each provider family $f$ (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google), let $M_f$ be its model set and $A_f$ its non-baseline agents.  The baseline scaffold is Terminus~2.

\textit{Model effect} (fixing scaffold): the score range across models on Terminus~2,
\begin{equation}
  \Delta_{\mathrm{model}}^{(f,b)}
  = \max_{m \in M_f}\, s(m,\,\text{terminus-2},\,b)
  - \min_{m \in M_f}\, s(m,\,\text{terminus-2},\,b),
  \label{eq:model-effect}
\end{equation}
where $f$ denotes the provider family, $b$ is the benchmark, and $M_f$ is the set of models belonging to family $f$.  This measures how much performance varies due to model choice alone, with scaffold held fixed.

\textit{Agent effect} (fixing model): for each $(m, a)$ pair with both scores observed,
\begin{equation}
  \delta_{\mathrm{agent}}^{(m,a,b)}
  = \bigl|\, s(m,\,a,\,b) - s(m,\,\text{terminus-2},\,b) \,\bigr|,
  \label{eq:agent-delta}
\end{equation}
where $m$ is a specific model, $a$ is a non-baseline scaffold, and the absolute difference isolates the scaffold's marginal contribution for a fixed model on benchmark $b$.

The family-level agent effect averages over all available model--scaffold pairs:
\begin{equation}
  \Delta_{\mathrm{agent}}^{(f,b)}
  = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_{f,b}|}
  \sum_{(m,a)\in \mathcal{P}_{f,b}}
  \delta_{\mathrm{agent}}^{(m,a,b)},
  \label{eq:agent-effect}
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal{P}_{f,b}$ is the set of (model, scaffold) pairs in family $f$ for which both the scaffolded score $s(m, a, b)$ and the baseline score $s(m, \text{terminus-2}, b)$ are observed.

A benchmark is \emph{model-dominant} for family $f$ if $\Delta_{\mathrm{model}}^{(f,b)} > \Delta_{\mathrm{agent}}^{(f,b)}$.  Family-level summaries average across benchmarks:
\begin{align}
  \overline{\Delta}_{\mathrm{model}}^{(f)}
  &= \frac{1}{|B_f|}\sum_{b \in B_f} \Delta_{\mathrm{model}}^{(f,b)}, &
  \overline{\Delta}_{\mathrm{agent}}^{(f)}
  &= \frac{1}{|B_f|}\sum_{b \in B_f} \Delta_{\mathrm{agent}}^{(f,b)},
  \label{eq:family-summary}
\end{align}
where $B_f$ is the set of benchmarks for which family $f$ has sufficient coverage to compute both effects.

\begin{table}[t]
  \centering
  \caption{Within-family model vs.\ agent effect.  Model effect: score range across models on Terminus~2.  Agent effect: mean $|\Delta|$ from switching scaffold.}
  \label{tab:within-family-summary}
  \begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
    \toprule
    Family & Models & Agent & $\overline{\Delta}_{\mathrm{model}}$ & $\overline{\Delta}_{\mathrm{agent}}$ & Ratio & Model-dom.\ \% \\
    \midrule
    Anthropic & 3 & claude-code & \AnthropicModelEffectMean{} & \AnthropicAgentEffectMean{} & \AnthropicModelAgentRatio{}$\times$ & \AnthropicModelWinPct\% \\
    OpenAI & 3 & codex & \OpenAIModelEffectMean{} & \OpenAIAgentEffectMean{} & \OpenAIModelAgentRatio{}$\times$ & \OpenAIModelWinPct\% \\
    Google & 2 & gemini-cli & \GoogleModelEffectMean{} & \GoogleAgentEffectMean{} & \GoogleModelAgentRatio{}$\times$ & \GoogleModelWinPct\% \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

\textit{The model dominates in all families with $\ge 3$ models.}  Anthropic and OpenAI show \AnthropicModelAgentRatio{}$\times$ and \OpenAIModelAgentRatio{}$\times$ model-to-agent ratios respectively, with model-dominant classification on \AnthropicModelWinPct{}\% and \OpenAIModelWinPct{}\% of benchmarks.  Google's smaller model set (2 models) yields a near-parity ratio (\GoogleModelAgentRatio{}$\times$), suggesting that the measured model effect scales with intra-family model diversity.
